title: The crowds were astonished (Matthew 7:28–29)
hookLine: he taught as one with authority; the sermon has unsettled people for two thousand years

cards: Some words follow a person out the door. A speech, a song, a hard conversation, and the drive home happens with the radio off, because nothing else will fit. For thirty days this path has sat on a hillside in Galilee.
Blessed are the meek. Salt and light. Love your enemies.
Give in secret. Our Father. The birds, the lilies, the plank, the narrow gate, the house on the rock.
Now the sermon is over. Jesus stops talking. Matthew doesn't tell us what anyone said next.

teach.b: The last lines, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes."
Astonished is a strong word. The Greek means something like struck, knocked out of your ordinary way of thinking. Not impressed.
Matthew says it was his authority. The Greek is exousia, the right and the power to act. The scribes were respected teachers of the law.
Matthew doesn't spell out the contrast, but some readers point out that later Jewish teaching often grounded a ruling in the teachers who came before, a careful and humble way to teach.
On this hillside, Jesus kept saying something different: ye have heard that it was said, "But I say unto you." He spoke as if the words were his to give. And then the content.
Turn the other cheek. Love your enemy. Don't worry.
People have been unsettled by this sermon ever since. Some Christians take it very literally, and a few traditions refuse to swear oaths or bear arms because of it.

Others read it as the shape of life in God's kingdom, a goal no one reaches alone. In the 1930s, the German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a book on it, and he paid for his convictions with his life.
Martin Luther King Jr. drew on its love for enemies in the civil rights movement. Matthew doesn't end with the crowd at ease. He ends with them astonished.

how: Some Christians return to the Sermon on the Mount again and again, reading Matthew 5 to 7 in one sitting, and some traditions shape their whole way of life around it.

games.q: the sermon has ended. you're in the crowd. what does Matthew say you feel?
games.why: "the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes."

practice: Reread the Beatitudes, the sermon's opening: Matthew chapter five, verses three to twelve, if you have a Bible or a phone nearby.
If not, take just the first one: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Let one line land, and without arguing with it, notice where it presses.

wordCard.voice: Exousia, the Greek word for authority, the right and the power to act. The crowds were knocked off balance by a teacher who spoke with it, and by what he said.

orig.note: Greek: authority, the right and power to act.

carryVoice: Your line: let it unsettle you. That's the end of the Sermon on the Mount, and tomorrow the path walks out into the desert. Day two hundred sixty-one, done.
